translationRepairs: During the Dazhun era the Martial Emperor's general Li Cunxiao, having pacified Xing and Ming, proposed to the Martial Emperor that Zhen and Ding be seized together, and for years thereafter led campaigns harassing the counties under Zhen.

During the Dashun era the Martial Emperor's general Li Cunxiao, having pacified Xing and Ming, proposed to the Martial Emperor that Zhen and Ding be seized together, and for years thereafter led campaigns harassing the counties under Zhen.
Focus unit opens 大順中; 順 is shùn, so Dashun is the correct era name and Dazhun is a false reading. The proposed idiomatic line otherwise matches the Chinese.

In the Dazhun era the Martial Emperor's general Li Cunxiao, having pacified Xing and Ming, offered a plan to the Martial Emperor to annex Zhen and Ding, and thereafter for years led campaigns to harass Zhen's subordinate counties.

In the Dashun era the Martial Emperor's general Li Cunxiao, having pacified Xing and Ming, offered a plan to the Martial Emperor to annex Zhen and Ding, and thereafter for years led campaigns to harass Zhen's subordinate counties.
Same era name error in the literal field: 大順 must be Dashun, not Dazhun; the rest of the proposed literal sentence is faithful.

Under Emperor Zhaozong Rong was granted the title Meritorious Minister of Lasting Concord, Preservation, and Endurance, rose to military governor of the Chengde army, Grand Preceptor, Director of the Chancellery, and Prince of Zhao; the Founding Emperor of Liang later added Minister of Works.

Under Emperor Zhaozong, Rong was granted the title Meritorious Minister of Lasting Concord, Preservation, and Endurance, rose to military governor of the Chengde army, Grand Preceptor, Director of the Chancellery, and Prince of Zhao; the Founding Emperor of Liang later added Minister of Works.
Chinese 鎔於昭宗朝 treats Rong and Zhaozong as distinct; without the comma English 'Emperor Zhaozong Rong' fuses them into one name. The comma fixes that real ambiguity without changing meaning.

In the reign of Emperor Zhaozong Rong was granted the title Meritorious Minister of Lasting Concord, Preservation, and Endurance, rose to military governor of the Chengde army, Grand Preceptor, Director of the Chancellery, and Prince of Zhao; the Founding Emperor of Liang added Minister of Works.

In the reign of Emperor Zhaozong, Rong was granted the title Meritorious Minister of Lasting Concord, Preservation, and Endurance, rose to military governor of the Chengde army, Grand Preceptor, Director of the Chancellery, and Prince of Zhao; the Founding Emperor of Liang added Minister of Works.
Literal field has the same fusion of Zhaozong and Rong; 鎔於昭宗朝 requires separating the emperor's reign from Rong as subject.

The Bian general Zhang Cunjing attacked the city with scaling ladders and battering rams massed like clouds. Chuzhi mounted the wall and called out, "Our humble district has never been disloyal to the court nor discourteous to neighboring prefectures. Why did we not expect Your Lordship to enter our land?"

The Bian general Zhang Cunjing attacked the city with scaling ladders and battering rams massed like clouds. Chuzhi mounted the wall and called out, "Our humble district has never been disloyal to the court nor discourteous to neighboring prefectures. I did not expect Your Lordship to enter our land—why?"

不虞君之涉吾地，何也 states surprise that the addressee entered the land and asks why; the original English wrongly turns this into self-blame about failing to expect the invasion. The proposed rendering matches the Chinese.

The Bian general Zhang Cunjing attacked the city; scaling ladders and battering rams massed like clouds; Chuzhi mounted the wall and called out, "Our humble district has never been disloyal to the court nor discourteous to neighboring prefectures—why did we not expect Your Lordship to enter our land?"

The Bian general Zhang Cunjing attacked the city; scaling ladders and battering rams massed like clouds; Chuzhi mounted the wall and called out, "Our humble district has never been disloyal to the court nor discourteous to neighboring prefectures—I did not expect Your Lordship to enter our land—why?"
Literal likewise misreads 不虞…何也 as 'why did we not expect'; the Chinese asserts unexpected invasion and questions the reason. The replacement is accurate.

既至湖湘 refers to the Hunan (Dongting–Xiang) region, not Hunan plus Hubei; the idiomatic already has Hunan, and dropping Hubei from the literal restores the Chinese scope.

At the beginning of Tiancheng, An Chonghui knew his origins and entrusted him to Duan Huai to raise as a son;
付段佪 names Duan Huai (佪 = huái); Duan Si invents a wrong given name. The added comma after Tiancheng is needed English punctuation and does not alter sense.

Literal repeats the false name Duan Si for 段佪; Duan Huai is correct, with the comma after the reign phrase.
Si knew this was unsuitable and allowed him to go as he pleased.
Huai knew this was unsuitable and allowed him to go as he pleased.
Short-form subject 佪 continues 段佪 from the prior unit; English Si does not match that given name, while Huai does.

Literal likewise mistranslates 佪 as Si; the short form is Huai, continuing 段佪.
